content: Nitroglycerin ointment is prescribed to prevent chest pain, also known as angina. It achieves this by relaxing the blood vessels leading to the heart, thereby increasing the supply of blood and oxygen to the heart. This medication may also be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Nitroglycerin ointment is applied to the skin and is typically used three to six times a day. Your doctor may instruct you to remove the ointment at a specific time each day. Follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully, and ask your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Use the ointment exactly as directed. Do not apply more or less than prescribed, and do not use it more frequently than instructed. While nitroglycerin ointment helps control chest pain, it does not cure it. Continue using the medication even if you feel well, and do not stop using it without consulting your doctor, as abrupt discontinuation may cause chest pain. The ointment comes with a special paper marked with a ruled line to measure the dose in inches. Squeeze the prescribed amount of ointment onto the paper and spread it in a thin layer over a relatively hair-free area of skin, such as your chest, covering an area of at least 2 inches by 3 inches. Do not rub the ointment into the skin. Leave the paper on top of the ointment and secure it in place with an elastic bandage, hosiery, or tape. Wash your hands after application, avoiding contact with the ointment on your fingers. Nitroglycerin can lose its effectiveness over time, a phenomenon known as tolerance. If your angina attacks become more frequent, last longer, or are more severe, contact your doctor immediately. Nitroglycerin is also used to improve circulation in patients with Raynaud's disease. Discuss the potential risks of using this medication for your condition with your doctor. Before using nitroglycerin ointment, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to nitroglycerin in any form, isosorbide, or any other drugs. Also, disclose if you are taking medications such as sildenafil (Viagra) or vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have or have ever had anemia, glaucoma, or recent head trauma. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using this medication, contact your doctor immediately. If you are undergoing surgery, including dental surgery, inform the healthcare provider that you are using nitroglycerin ointment. Be aware that this medication may cause drowsiness or dizziness. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how it affects you. Ask your doctor about the safe use of alcohol while using this medication, as alcohol can exacerbate its side effects. If you miss a dose, apply it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not apply a double dose to make up for a missed one. Common side effects of nitroglycerin ointment include headache, skin irritation or rash, dizziness, upset stomach, and flushing (a sensation of warmth). If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects, such as blurred vision, dry mouth, chest pain, or fainting, require immediate medical attention. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA's MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store this medication out of reach of children and away from toothpaste or other ointments and creams. Close the ointment tube tightly after each use. Store it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture (not in the bathroom). Dispose of outdated or no longer needed medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Nitroglycerin ointment is not intended for acute angina attacks. Continue using nitroglycerin tablets or spray for chest pain that has already started. If headaches persist, consult your doctor about taking acetaminophen. Your nitroglycerin dose may need adjustment. Do not take aspirin or other headache medications while using nitroglycerin ointment unless directed by your doctor. If skin irritation continues, apply the ointment to a different area of skin. Do not share this medication with others. Consult your pharmacist with any questions about refilling your prescription.
